source_title: Quaker Oats Takes Big Loss On Sale Of Snapple Business (The Seattle Times / wire report)
publisher_issuer: The Seattle Times (wire-service report, 1997); corroborated by Harvard Business Review (How Snapple Got Its Juice Back) and contemporaneous business press; Quaker Oats filed Form 8-K with the SEC on the sale
company_context: Quaker Oats acquired the Snapple beverage brand in 1994 for about $1.7 billion (outbidding rivals), intending to plug it into the mass-market supermarket distribution machine that had built Gatorade into a billion-dollar brand. The strategy mismatched Snapple's independent direct-store-delivery distributor network and quirky brand identity; Quaker sold Snapple to Triarc in 1997 for about $300 million.
business_type: Consumer packaged goods - branded ready-to-drink beverages; distribution-channel-dependent brand equity
macro_context: Mid-1990s ready-to-drink beverage growth; channel conflict between mass-grocery distribution and independent direct-store-delivery distributors that built alternative beverage brands.
evidence_summary: Quaker Oats paid about $1.7 billion for Snapple in 1994, then attempted to force the brand into its Gatorade-style mass-supermarket distribution system, disrupting Snapple's network of independent distributors who sold through delis, bodegas, and convenience outlets and alienating the brand's customer base. In 1997 Quaker sold Snapple to Triarc Beverages for about $300 million, recording a charge of about $1.4 billion related to the loss on the sale. The debacle cost Quaker's chairman and president their jobs and hastened Quaker's loss of independence (later acquired by PepsiCo). The losses were driven by a deliberate, wrong strategic/distribution action layered onto the acquired brand.

source_backed_metrics.executive_departures: chairman and president lost their jobs

owner_decision_context: Quaker leadership assumed Snapple's growth could be replicated through the same mass-grocery distribution and marketing playbook that scaled Gatorade, underweighting that Snapple's equity depended on its independent distributor channel and counter-culture identity.
action_taken: Acquired Snapple for about $1.7 billion, restructured its distribution and marketing toward Quaker's mass-market model, then sold it for about $300 million in 1997 and took an approximately $1.4 billion charge.
outcome_evidence: Sale at about $300 million versus about $1.7 billion paid, an approximately $1.4 billion charge, and the ouster of top executives confirm the post-acquisition channel/strategy actions worsened the position rather than improving it.
source_limitations: WebFetch of the Seattle Times archive and the related SEC 8-K returns HTTP 403 here; figures verified from search snippets across multiple credible sources (Seattle Times wire report, Harvard Business Review, Museum of Failure) rather than full-text read. The approximately $1.4 billion figure is the reported charge/loss on sale; the original purchase price is sometimes cited as $1.7 billion (1994).
directly_stated: Quaker paid about $1.7 billion for Snapple in 1994
Quaker sold Snapple to Triarc for about $300 million in 1997
Quaker took a charge of about $1.4 billion on the sale
The debacle cost the chairman and president their jobs and preceded Quaker's loss of independence
inferred: The proximate driver was a go-to-market / distribution-channel mismatch imposed after acquisition
This is a wrong-action-worsened (outcome 10) strategic capex/M&A and GTM failure, not a market-demand collapse
